Whoever succeeds in achieving this present spiritual
victory will also be the most capable in working at the task
of building for the future; for such a one will not be in turns
excited and depressed, but will accomplish his work with
inner serenity and cheerfulness of spirit. But who is it, who
conscious of living on this victorious level can echo the words
of Paul: "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed;
perplexed, but not driven to despair"?
The spiritual strength of Paul springs from the fact that he
lives in two worlds; not only in the visible world of change
and decay, of tears and death, that world in which we are
"afflicted in every way" and "perplexed"
, but also in the
invisible world in which there is no fear and no despair.
From this invisible world he derives the power to master all
those pains and trials which flow from the visible and
temporal. In fact we may go further and add that the trials
of the visible and temporal scene serve to make him all the
more certain of invisible realities: "We have this treasure
in earthen vessels, to show that the transcendent power
belongs to God and not to us."
The fact that man lives in two worlds is not a distinctively
Christian insight. Everywhere and at every time in which
man has transcended his anxiety about his bodily existence,
about the material security of his life, has opened the "eye
of the soul" and in inner spiritual vision has caught a glimpse
of the world of the spirit, then he has lived in two worlds and
then two worlds have dwelt in his breast. At such moments
the world of the spirit, the world of beauty, truth and good-
ness shines upon him in its inspiring splendour and instils
into him the sense of utter obligation towards it. He learns
to understand that it is not the exigencies of the passing day,
